title: Sleeman Centre ice allocation and youth subsidy
subtitle: Councillor pay set for next term, farmland protection bill supported, development charge and property tax updates approved.
overview: Council's longest discussion was the Sleeman Centre operating model. Council gave staff authority to negotiate rates and fees where revenue can be recovered, and raised the capital reserve ticket service charge to between $2.00 and $3.00 from September 1, 2026. It rejected ending the Youth Facility Discount at the Sleeman Centre {{vote:m13}}, so the youth subsidy stays. Delegates from minor and girls hockey said ice is scarce and asked to keep their bookings. Council also asked staff to report on extending youth subsidies to other facilities and on low-barrier recreation programs.

Council set the City Councillor salary at $59,137 for the 2026-2030 term, with annual increases tied to the non-union municipal employee rate {{vote:m18}}. Council also supported provincial Bill 21, the Protect Our Food Act, 2025, to protect farmland.

The consent agenda approved a development charges update, the 2026 property tax policy and a recreation facilities allocation process. Council received the annual reports of the Integrity Commissioner and Lobbyist Registrar. After a closed session on a bargaining mandate for Ontario Public Service Employees Local 231, the mayor reported that Council gave direction to staff.

decisions.detail: Council defeated the proposal to end the Youth Facility Discount for Sleeman Centre rentals, so the discount remains {{vote:m13}}.

decisions.item: Sleeman Centre rates and fees authority
decisions.detail: The Deputy CAO of Public Services, or designate, may negotiate Sleeman Centre rates and fees when revenue can be recovered through rental profit share or ticket sales.
The capital reserve fund ticket service charge rises to between $2.00 and $3.00 starting September 1, 2026.
The City Councillor salary is set at $59,137 for the 2026-2030 term, with annual increases equal to the non-union municipal employee rate {{vote:m18}}.
Staff will report through the 2027 budget process on extending the youth subsidy to facilities including, but not limited to, River Run Centre and Guelph Museums.
Staff will report on the financial impact of Parks and Recreation Master Plan recommendations for low-barrier access for underserved groups.
Council approved the 2026 Development Charges Update Study, an amending by-law, an updated interest policy and a Local Service Policy update by May 27, 2027.
Council supports the farmland protection bill and will send its resolution to provincial ministers, an MPP and agriculture and municipal associations.

debate: Hockey delegates said Guelph has too little ice for its population and that the Sleeman Centre is essential capacity. They objected to losing multi-month bookings and the youth subsidy, said they were not consulted, and offered to move for events with notice.

Staff said groups would be moved to guaranteed blocks at the new south end centre, with no loss of ice time during the transition. They said long-term blocks and displacement clauses would hamper bookings, and that the Sleeman Centre needs more events, including for downtown business.

On the youth discount, some councillors favoured removing it to free up the Sleeman Centre and said the new allocation policy addresses equity. Others said the cost was small, noted the transition period, and opposed cutting youth sport support.

On pay, supporters of the increase said Guelph's per-councillor workload, cost of living and diversity of candidates matter, and that comparators change. Opponents said Guelph already pays more than similar single-tier cities such as Barrie and Kingston. A delegate urged a pay freeze.
On Bill 21, one councillor supported the farmland protection goal but doubted the bill would advance provincially and noted farmer concerns.
